summary:
We developed an interactive decision-support platform for exploring potential lunar landing and operating locations. The system combines NASA lunar topography, illumination, temperature, radiation and other environmental resources with Earth terrain data. Two CNN-based workflows compare lunar terrain with interpretable Earth analogues and estimate terrain mobility for rovers and humans using features such as elevation, slope and roughness.

Through the web application, users can explore candidate lunar regions, inspect physical measurements and environmental ratings, compare terrain patches, and upload their own environmental scenarios for mobility assessment. Rather than presenting an unexplained suitability score, the platform shows the evidence, model outputs and caveats behind each result.

Our project addresses the difficulty of understanding unfamiliar lunar environments by transforming complex scientific datasets into an accessible and interactive experience. It is intended as an exploratory decision-support tool to help researchers and the public investigate why one lunar location may be more operationally promising than another.
details:
Lunar Exploration & Assessment Platform (LEAP) is an interactive decision-support prototype for exploring potential operating areas near the lunar south pole. It combines terrain analysis, machine learning, environmental indicators, and Earth analog retrieval in one web application. Rather than providing a single arbitrary score, the platform allows users to inspect the evidence, comparisons and limitations behind each result.

We processed seven lunar regions and five Earth regions into consistent 960 m × 960 m terrain patches. Each patch is represented by raster channels describing relative elevation, slope, roughness at different scales, and local surface shape. A terrain-similarity CNN converts these channels into numerical embeddings and retrieves Earth patches with similar terrain structure. The application also reports physical differences so that cosine similarity is not mistaken for a safety percentage.

A separate multi-task CNN estimates terrain mobility. It was trained and tested on geographically separated Earth patches using provisional labels generated from slope-based route connectivity. Its outputs include rover operability, terrain-only human walkability, and crossing predictions along four axes. We then apply the Earth-trained model to lunar terrain as experimental inference. However, they do not represent actual safety or astronaut safety. Instead, they help to identify areas that deserve a closer review.

The project also includes an environmental scoring workflow. Direct LOLA map products provide regional or tile-level indicators for solar illumination, Earth visibility, permanent shadow, and visible sky. The scorer can also accept temperature, radiation, plasma, dust, seismic, exosphere, and soil inputs. In the current demonstration, many non-map environmental values are controlled fixtures or regional references rather than verified measurements for every patch, and the interface labels these limitations. Missing or unsupported evidence is treated as Unknown rather than as zero or suitable.

Our main benefit is that several difficult datasets can be examined through one accessible interface. Scientists and planners can compare terrain, inspect directional mobility, find possible Earth training analogs, and review environmental domains without manually combining many rasters and tables. The intended impact is to support early-stage screening, public understanding, analogue-field planning, and more focused scientific investigation. It does not replace engineering qualification or mission review.

We developed the data and machine-learning pipelines primarily in Python using PyTorch, NumPy, pandas, SciPy, Rasterio, PyProj, Shapely, Jupyter, and ONNX Runtime. The web application uses React, TypeScript, Vite, Leaflet, and Pyodide. We used NASA lunar products from LRO LOLA, enhanced south-polar topography models, and related environmental archives, alongside Earth elevation, land-cover, climate, and OpenStreetMap data. We used OpenAI ChatGPT Codex and Claude code as development assistants for brainstorming, research planning, data interpretation, code generation, debugging and documentation editing.

The creative aspect of our project is the connection between unfamiliar lunar terrain and interpretable Earth locations, combined with directional mobility and environmental evidence under a shared patch system. The application also allows users to upload their own environmental scenarios and run them through the mobility model, turning the project from a fixed set of results into an exploratory assessment tool. Predictions are presented alongside supporting measurements so users can see both the evidence behind each result and the limits of what the system can conclude.

Important design considerations centred on making the web application understandable, interactive and transparent. We designed the interface so users can explore candidate lunar regions, compare them with familiar Earth terrain, inspect mobility and environmental ratings, and upload their own environmental scenarios for assessment. Instead of presenting a single unexplained score, the application shows the supporting measurements, model outputs and relevant caveats behind each result.
